sections.title: Cold
sections.html:
Le-khatḥila, one must be careful that permitted foods do not touch forbidden ones, nor meat touch cheese. If they did touch and both were dry and cold, they are permitted without rinsing. If there is a concern that crumbs of one stuck to the other, one should rub the place where they touched in order to remove them. If there was moisture or greasiness at the place where they touched, one must remove everything that stuck there by rinsing, and when necessary also by rubbing. If meat touched soft cheese that cannot be rinsed, one must remove from the cheese and discard everything that touched the meat, and the meat must be rinsed (Ḥullin 107b; SA 91:1; Shakh 1; Pitḥei Teshuva 1).

Bread that touched moist meat may be eaten with meat. If one wishes to eat it with milk, since the bread cannot be rinsed without becoming repulsive, one must scrape off from the bread whatever touched the meat. Likewise, bread that touched moist cheese, if one wishes to eat it with meat, one must scrape off from it whatever touched the cheese (SA 91:3; Pitḥei Teshuva 4).

If a piece of meat fell into milk, if they are cold there is no absorption, and one must take out the piece of meat and rinse it well, and it is permitted (SA 91:4). The milk is also permitted, because even if a little moisture from the meat mixed into the milk, it is nullified in sixty.

Some are stringent and hold that all this applies on condition that the piece of meat was raw, but if the cold meat was cooked or roasted, it may absorb milk in its outer layer, and therefore one must remove from it kedei kelipa (the thickness of a peel), and the rest is permitted. And if the cooked or roasted meat has cracks, or it is seasoned with a sharp spice, even though it is cold, the milk may be absorbed throughout it, and as long as this does not involve a great loss, all of it is forbidden (Rema 91:7).1

sections.title: Cooking in a Keli Rishon
sections.html:
Cooking takes place in a keli rishon (primary vessel), that is, in a pot standing on a fire or another source of heat. The power of cooking, through heat and liquids, is that it mixes the flavors of foods into one another. Therefore if, for example, one cooked non-kosher meat with legumes, their flavors mix into one another, and therefore if the permitted food does not contain sixty times the forbidden food, the entire mixture is forbidden (above 34:3-4).

Even after the vessel has been removed from the fire, or the fire under it has gone out, since it was heated on the fire, it is still considered a keli rishon that can cook. This is on condition that its heat is at least yad soledet bo (the heat from which the hand recoils) (SA 105:2; 45° Celsius, see Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 10:4). But if its heat dropped below this temperature, it does not cook, and the law of foods placed into it is like the law of cold foods that fell into one another (as explained in halakha 1; the law of pickled food will be explained in halakha 9).

And although often a keli rishon that is not on the fire does not have the power to cook, to expel the flavor in the forbidden piece and to cause it to be absorbed into the permitted foods, since it sometimes does have the power to cook, the Sages established a rule: as long as there is no reliable gentile who tasted and said that there is no taste of the forbidden food in the permitted foods, one must regard everything in the keli rishon as if it had been fully cooked. And if the permitted food does not contain sixty times the forbidden piece, then even after the forbidden piece is taken out, the dish is forbidden (this will be explained further below in halakha 5; see also above 34:4).2

sections.title: Irui (Pouring) from a Keli Rishon
sections.html:
If one poured what was cooked in a keli rishon onto other foods, the irui (pouring) has the power to cook them kedei kelipa. For example, if one poured boiling non-kosher gravy onto meat, the surface of the meat becomes forbidden and must be peeled off, and the rest of the meat must be rinsed well and is permitted to eat. Kedei kelipa is the thinnest layer of the food that can be peeled off in one piece.

If one poured hot water from a keli rishon onto a kosher piece of meat and a piece of nevela, flavor can pass from the nevela into the kosher piece kedei kelipa, because irui can expel and cause absorption simultaneously. Therefore, one must remove the outer layer of the kosher meat and discard it, and rinse the rest well (SA 68:10).3

sections.title: Keli Sheni, Keli Shelishi and Gush
sections.html:
A keli sheni (secondary vessel) is the vessel into which a dish was poured from the vessel that stood on the fire, and since its walls were not heated on the fire like a keli rishon, the hot dish in it does not have the power to cook. And even though it is still scalding, since the walls of the vessel cool it, it does not have the power to cook. However, le-khatḥila we take into account the opinion of those who hold that it has the power to expel and cause absorption of flavors kedei kelipa, and if, for example, a zucchini fell into non-kosher soup in a keli sheni, one peels the zucchini and the rest is kosher (SA 105:2; above halakha 1).

A keli shelishi (tertiary vessel) is the vessel into which a dish was poured from the keli sheni, and since it is removed by another degree from the source of heat, its power to mix flavors is weakened, and even if it is still very hot, there is no concern that it will cause absorption and expulsion kedei kelipa in foods placed in it. Likewise, there is no concern that irui from a keli sheni causes flavors to be absorbed and expelled; rather, its law is like cold.4

Gush (a solid mass of food): Some say that everything we have learned, that a keli sheni does not cook, applies only to a dish that is not solid, such as a liquid dish that comes into full contact with the cold walls of the vessel and cools down, or a dish that crumbles, and the air that enters it cools it. But a solid food, such as a piece of meat, a pashtida (casserole) or a potato, retains its heat within it, and even though it was transferred from a keli rishon to a keli sheni or shelishi or beyond, it is not so affected by the walls, and as long as its heat is yad soledet bo, it has the power to cook, or at least to cause flavor to be absorbed throughout the food it touched. And some say there is no difference between solid and liquid, and that the heat of a solid food too is preserved only by virtue of its being in the vessel in which it was cooked, and from the moment it was transferred to another vessel its heat steadily weakens and it is unable to cook or to cause flavors to be absorbed. Le-khatḥila one should act in accordance with the stringent opinion, and in a situation of great loss, in accordance with the lenient opinion (Ḥokhmat Adam 60:12).5

sections.title: Explanation of the Rules of Mixtures
sections.html:
The rules that the Sages established in the laws of mixtures and absorptions, such as “nullification in sixty” and “a keli rishon cooks,” are fences that the Sages set in order to distance a person from cases in which he would eat food in which a forbidden taste can be detected. But the intention is not to determine that always, or in most cases, the forbidden taste can be detected in accordance with the rules.

That is to say, although often the forbidden taste is nullified in a quantity forty times greater than it, since in remote cases, when the forbidden taste is strong, it is nullified only in sixty, the Sages determined that all prohibitions are nullified in sixty. Therefore, if a piece of non-kosher meat fell into a dish, although often its taste is nullified in forty, as long as the dish does not contain sixty times the forbidden piece, all of it is forbidden.

Not only that, but if the dish did not contain sixty times the non-kosher piece that fell into it, even though it was taken out of the dish, the dish remains forbidden, out of concern that perhaps the entire flavor of the non-kosher piece came out into it. Not only that, but if that same non-kosher piece falls again into a second dish that also does not contain sixty times it, that dish too becomes forbidden. That is, we are concerned that perhaps all the flavor came out into the first dish, and that perhaps all the flavor came out into the second dish. And so too with a third dish (SA and Rema 98:4).

Moreover, the rule does not distinguish between whether the non-kosher piece stayed in the dish for a minute or for an hour (above note 2), because there is no way to determine how much flavor comes out in a minute and how much in an hour. Not only that, but even if the dish was removed from the fire, although its heat weakened, since it sometimes still has the power to cook as when it was on the fire, the Sages established a rule that even a keli rishon that is not on the fire cooks, and therefore if the non-kosher piece falls into it and it does not contain sixty times that piece, all of it becomes forbidden.

That is to say, the rules set a fence for situations of doubt in order to distance a person from the prohibition, but they do not determine that this is the actual situation. Therefore, if a reliable gentile tastes the dish and says that no forbidden taste can be detected in it, the doubt is resolved and there is no longer any need to use the rules of the fence, and the mixture is permitted even though it does not contain sixty times the forbidden food (above 34:4). But when it is not possible to ask a reliable gentile, one must act according to the safety rules. And since the gentile's answer has sometimes been found to be inaccurate, the custom is not to rely on a gentile, except in cases of great loss (above 34:5).

It also seems right to explain that all the disputes among the Rishonim and Aḥaronim in the laws of mixtures and absorptions, such as regarding irui from a keli rishon, a keli sheni and gush, concern the question of how far the fence must be extended in order to prevent a stumbling. The main approach in halakha is that the rules of the fence are intended to fence off even remote cases, but not to be excessively stringent and fence off extremely rare cases. And if in practice someone encounters a rare case in which the prohibition was nullified according to the rules and nevertheless its taste can be detected, he should stop eating. As for what he already ate, he did not transgress a prohibition, since he acted according to the guidance of the Sages and did not intend to eat something forbidden.6

sections.title: Roasting
sections.html:
Two pieces of meat, one kosher and the other non-kosher, were roasted or baked together on the fire while touching each other, whether they were one on top of the other or one beside the other. If one of them was fatty, that is, it contained fat, then by means of the fat the forbidden taste spreads and penetrates the entire permitted piece, and therefore if it does not contain sixty times the forbidden piece, all of it is forbidden. If both were lean, since there is no fat there to spread throughout the piece, one must remove from the permitted piece kedei netila, that is, the width of a finger (1.9 cm), and the rest is kosher (SA 105:4-5).

Since in practice it is often difficult to define the condition of the fat, the custom is to be stringent according to both possibilities: if the permitted piece does not contain sixty times the forbidden food, all of it is forbidden, lest one of the pieces is fatty; and if the permitted piece does contain sixty times the forbidden food, one must remove kedei netila from it, lest both are lean. All this applies to kinds of meat, where there is almost always doubt about their fattiness, but with other foods, when it is entirely clear that both pieces are lean, one need only remove kedei netila from the kosher piece (Rema 105:5; Zivḥei Tzedek 43).7

sections.title: Tata'a Gavar – The Lower One Prevails
sections.html:
We have learned so far that with cold foods there is no absorption, whereas with cooking in a keli rishon there is complete absorption. The question is what the law is when a cold food and a hot food were placed one on the other. In practice it was ruled: tata'a gavar, that is, the lower one prevails, because the nature of heat is to rise upward. Therefore, if there was hot soup in a keli rishon, and cold tereifa meat fell into it, since the lower one prevails, we are concerned that complete cooking took place there, and if the soup does not contain sixty times the non-kosher piece, it becomes forbidden. If the kosher soup was cold and hot tereifa meat fell into it, since the lower one prevails, we are not concerned about complete cooking, but we are concerned about absorption to the extent of kedei kelipa, and therefore it suffices for the soup to contain sixty times the outer layer of the tereifa meat (Pesaḥim 76a, following Shmuel; SA 105:3).

Similarly, if two pieces of meat were placed one on top of the other, one kosher and one tereifa: if the lower one is hot at the level of a keli rishon, even if they are not on the fire, the severity of the contact between them is like the severity of the cooking of fatty roasted meat (as explained in the previous halakha), and consequently, if the kosher piece does not contain sixty times more than the forbidden one, all of it has become forbidden. If the lower one is cold, the power of the lower one prevails and the contact between them does not have the severity of cooking; however, since the upper piece is hot, there is absorption there kedei kelipa, and one must peel the kosher piece at the place where it touched the tereifa.8

sections.title: Salted Is Like Boiling
sections.html:
The Sages said: meli'aḥ ke-rote'aḥ (salted is like boiling). Salted food is food that is not eaten on its own because of how salty it is. The rule is that if the salted food touched another food and there is moisture between them, the salted food causes its flavor to be absorbed into the other food, similar to the absorption caused by boiling. This is because the salt causes the food to release moisture and flavor from within it and to cause them to be absorbed into the food it touches. However, the salted food itself does not take in flavor from the tafel (unsalted) piece. Therefore, if a salted piece of meat touched a piece of unsalted cheese, the salt in the meat causes the meat's flavor to go out into the cheese, but the unsalted cheese does not release flavor into the meat, and it suffices to rinse the meat and it is permitted. If the cheese was salted and the meat unsalted, the cheese imparts flavor to the meat, whereas the meat does not impart flavor to the cheese. And if both pieces are salted, both impart flavor to each other (Ḥullin 113a; Pesaḥim 76a).

And how much of the other piece does the salted piece render forbidden? If both were lean, without fattiness, the salted piece renders the unsalted one forbidden kedei kelipa; and if one of them was fatty, the salted piece renders the entire unsalted piece forbidden, because by means of the fattiness the taste of the salted piece spreads throughout the unsalted one. And if the unsalted piece was sixty times the size of the salted one, it does not become forbidden (SA 91:5-6). And since it is often difficult to determine whether one of them is fatty, the custom is to be stringent according to both possibilities (Rema 91:5; 105:9; above note 7). Therefore, if the piece that received flavor from the salted one contained sixty times it, its outer layer must be forbidden, for perhaps they are lean and its outer layer became forbidden; and if it does not contain sixty times it, all of it must be forbidden, because perhaps one of them is fatty.9

sections.title: Pickled Is Like Cooked
sections.html:
The Sages said that kavush (pickled, i.e. steeped) is considered like cooked; that is, when foods are steeped in liquids continuously for a full twenty-four hours, all the flavors of the foods in the liquids are absorbed into one another as in cooking. Therefore, if a kosher food and a non-kosher food were soaked in liquids for twenty-four hours, and there was not sixty times the non-kosher food, everything is forbidden.

If the steeping took place in very salty or sharp liquids, the steeping can take effect already within the amount of time it takes to bring them to a boil on a fire (SA 105:1). Many estimated this time at about 18 minutes. If the time of steeping was less than this, one must remove kedei kelipa from the kosher food (ibid.).

The poskim disagreed as to whether a vessel too absorbs flavor through steeping, for example, if non-kosher meat soup was soaked in a pot for twenty-four hours, whether the pot must be kashered. The halakha was ruled that le-khatḥila one should be stringent and kasher it by hagala, but if food has already been cooked in it, the food does not become forbidden.10

sections.title: Smell and Vapor
sections.html:
The Amoraim disagreed about the law of a kosher food that took in the smell of a forbidden food, for example, if a cake and fatty nevela meat were baked in one oven, and the smell of the nevela meat entered the cake, to the point that when eating the cake one senses the smell of the meat but does not detect its taste. In practice it was ruled that le-khatḥila one must be careful that the smell of a forbidden food not enter foods, but be-di'avad the smell does not render it forbidden, and the cake is kosher to eat.11

But if a great deal of vapor of a forbidden food entered a kosher food, for example if both were being cooked or baked in an oven and one cover completely covered both of them, since the vapor under the cover is very abundant, the vapor that comes out of the forbidden food renders the permitted food forbidden (Rema 108:1). Likewise, if one cooked non-kosher soup, and instead of covering the pot with a lid, covered it with zucchinis, the zucchinis that absorbed a great deal of vapor are forbidden (Rema 93:1).12
